title: This and That
description: Point at anything and ask what it is, then describe it: big or small, new or old, good or bad, hot or cold. The adjective learns to agree with the thing it describes, and 'that' is finally a different word from 'this'.
approach: Pointing game: the learner drags a hand cursor onto objects from Lessons 1 and 7 and hears هذا / هذي / ذاك, then flips adjective pairs on the same objects. Production on every card.
unlock_condition: ≥10/13 on the point-and-describe quiz and a recorded question-answer pair (وش هذا؟ — هذا …)
can_do: Describe things as big, small, new, old, good, bad, hot, cold

grammar.title: هذا، هذي، ذاك — this and that, he-things and she-things
grammar.explanation: Every Arabic thing is either he or she: words ending in ة (سيارة, قهوة, مدرسة) are she, nearly everything else is he. So 'this' has two forms — هذا for he-things, هذي for she-things — and you pick one by looking at the end of the word. For something further away use ذاك (or هذاك); for a she-thing far away, ذيك. For more than one thing, هذول. You can also glue this onto the noun as هالـ: هالكتاب, هالبيت — very Gulf, very common.

examples.english: This is a book and this is a car
This is my coffee and that is yours

grammar.title: Thing first, then the adjective — and it agrees
grammar.explanation: The describing word comes after the thing, not before: كتاب جديد is 'a new book' (book new). If the thing is a she-word, the adjective grows a ة too: سيارة جديدة. Add the article to both and you are still describing (الكتاب الجديد, the new book); put the article only on the thing and you have a full sentence: الكتاب جديد, the book is new — no word for 'is'. That is the same verbless sentence you built with pronouns in Lesson 4.

culture.title: Hot and cold are about drinks before weather
culture.note: Arabic coffee and tea are always served hot, even in August; only water, juice and لبن come cold. Asking for iced coffee at a majlis would puzzle the host. Cold water is the first thing offered to someone who has come in from the heat — ماي بارد — and the polite comment on the tea is that it is حار and حلو (hot and sweet), never that it is too hot. When the weather itself is the subject, people say الدنيا حر (the world is heat) rather than الجو حار.

vocabulary.teaching_note: For he-things and for men: هذا كتاب, هذا أخوي. You have heard it in every dialogue so far; now you own it. The ذ is the 'this' sound in English 'this', which makes it easy to remember.

vocabulary.video_hint: Someone holding up or pointing at an object while naming it; unboxings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: For she-things (words ending in ة) and for women: هذي سيارتي, هذي أختي. The MSA هذه is what you will see in print; هذي is what everyone says. Emiratis sometimes clip it to ذي.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing at a white car parked right beside the speaker.
vocabulary.video_hint: A vlogger presenting a feminine-word object (سيارة, شنطة, قهوة).

vocabulary.teaching_note: For things out of reach: ذاك البيت. Also هذاك. For she-things: ذيك / هذيك. The MSA ذلك is never said in the Gulf, so if you learned it, retire it now.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand pointing across a street at a house on the far side.
vocabulary.video_hint: Pointing at something across a room or street in a tour vlog.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The pointing question. وش is the Saudi 'what'; Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar say شنو هذا, the Emirates شو هذا, Jeddah إيش هذا, and Kuwaitis squeeze it to شهذا. Learn وش هذا and recognise the rest — the reply is always هذا + the thing.
vocabulary.image_scene: A child holding up an unfamiliar kitchen tool with a puzzled face, asking an adult.

example.english: What is this? — These are dates

vocabulary.video_hint: Children asking about objects; taste-test and unboxing videos.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Gulf says kibiir with an i. Feminine كبيرة kibiira, plural كبار. Of a person it also means old or senior: أخوي الكبير, my big brother.
vocabulary.image_scene: A very large white SUV next to a tiny hatchback, same street.
vocabulary.video_hint: House and car tours; size comparisons in challenges.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Feminine صغيرة, plural صغار. Of a person: young. Starts with the heavy ص — the same dark s as in صباح.
vocabulary.image_scene: A tiny handleless coffee cup next to a large mug.
vocabulary.video_hint: Small items held up; children described as صغار.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Saudi jidiid, upper Gulf يديد yidiid — the ج split again. Feminine جديدة. The Emirati greeting شو اليديد؟ (what's new?) is this word.
vocabulary.image_scene: A brand-new phone in an open box with the plastic film still on.
vocabulary.video_hint: Unboxings and new-car reveals; شو اليديد in Emirati greetings.

vocabulary.teaching_note: With the Gulf g: gadiim. For things, places and stories — an old house, an old phone. For an old person say كبير بالعمر, not قديم.
vocabulary.image_scene: A weathered wooden door with peeling paint in an old-town alley.
vocabulary.video_hint: Heritage-district tours; old vs new comparisons.

vocabulary.teaching_note: The Gulf good: زين. Also the answer to 'how are you' (زين الحمد لله) and 'is that OK?' (زين؟). Feminine زينة. كويس is understood but marks an outsider; خوش (good) goes before the noun in Kuwait: خوش ولد.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man tasting from a spoon and giving a thumbs-up, eyes closed in approval.
vocabulary.video_hint: Approval after tasting; زين as OK in any dialogue.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Originally 'rotten', now the everyday Gulf 'bad' for food, weather, a film, a day: الجو خايس. Most often people simply say مو زين (not good), which you will learn to build in Stage 2. Feminine خايسة.
vocabulary.image_scene: A man pulling a face at a plate of food he has just tasted.
vocabulary.video_hint: Complaints about weather, food or traffic in vlogs and sketches.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Hot to the touch or to drink: شاي حار. For spicy food the Gulf also says حار. For hot weather the phrase is الدنيا حر. Feminine حارة.
vocabulary.image_scene: Steam rising from a glass of tea, a hand pulling back from it.
vocabulary.video_hint: Tea or coffee just poured; spicy food reactions.

vocabulary.teaching_note: Cold to the touch or to drink: ماي بارد. Feminine باردة. Cold weather is برد (the noun): الدنيا برد. Also of a person — dull.
vocabulary.image_scene: A bottle of water beaded with condensation on a hot day.
vocabulary.video_hint: Cold drinks on a hot day; winter camping vlogs saying برد.

vocabulary.teaching_note: For more than one, whatever the gender: هذول ربعي, هذول كتبي. Also هذيل. The MSA هؤلاء is never heard. Far away: ذولاك.
vocabulary.image_scene: A hand gesturing at a group of three friends sitting together.
vocabulary.video_hint: Introducing a group; pointing at several items.

sound_spotlight.explanation: The soft th of English 'this' — and it lives in the Arabic word for this. The Gulf keeps it where Cairo says d; say it with the tongue tip touching the teeth and the voice on.
A heavy s made with the back of the tongue raised: the vowel after it turns dark, so صغير sounds nothing like سمك. Emphatics colour their neighbours; listen to the vowel, not just the consonant.
Fourth time now: قهوة, قهوة وحدة, صديق, قديم. If you hear qadiim with a formal q the speaker is reading, not talking.

lesson_sequence.detail: A majlis table with coffee, dates and objects from Lesson 1. One line of English: today you point and describe. Tap يلّا.
The learner drags a hand onto objects; the app says هذا or هذي depending on the word's ending, and ذاك for far objects. Then the learner hears one and taps the right object.
A native asks وش هذا؟ with a highlighted object; the learner records هذا / هذي + the word. The speech check listens for the right demonstrative.
Four pairs (big/small, new/old, good/bad, hot/cold) shown as two images each; audio plays the noun + adjective; the learner taps which image fits, then records the phrase with the ة where needed.
The learner records four sentences about their own objects: تلفوني جديد, بيتي صغير… from a menu.
The coffee-table dialogue plays; the learner takes Sara's lines on the second pass.
Thirteen items: point (audio → tap object), describe (noun + adjective → tap image), gender (هذا or هذي?). Counter rolls to 106. Nudge: describe three things around you.
